newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA WILL NOT COMPLETE NEW ATOMIC PLANT.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA WILL NOT COMPLETE NEW ATOMIC PLANT.

text.p: Bulgaria will not complete the construction of a new Soviet-designed nuclear power plant in Belene as it is an old design which does not match the new safety requirements, energy ministry officials said on Tuesday.

An experts council, in which the ministry, the Academy of Science and Energoproekt energy projects organisation were represented, discussed at a meeting late on Monday a technical study carried out by Russian firm Atomenergoproekt on the completion of the Belene plant.

"Most of the (Bulgarian) experts who were at the meeting were not happy with the technical and economic study, presented by Russian experts for building the 1,000-megawatt Soviet-designed reactor, which is on site," Energy Minister Georgi Stoilov told Reuters.
"In principle it is not reasonable to build a new 1,000-megawatt reactor," Stoilov said. "The reactor, we have on site, is an old generation," he added.

He said the meeting, which would continue its work later on Tuesday, planned to adopt a decision for updating Bulgaria's energy strategy until the year 2010. "Based on such a strategy, we can estimate whether the completion of the Belene plant would be worthwile," Stoilov said.
Other energy officials said under the council's decision a new generation reactor might be build in the future if the country needed more electricity supplies.

The construction of the Belene plant started in the 1980s. The foundations of the plant, which have been built before construction work was halted seven years ago due to a lack of cash and environmental protests, will stay, officials said.
Some 40 percent of the unit's main equipment including the 1,000 Soviet-designed reactor, have been supplied to Belene, 250 km (160 miles) north of Sofia.
Some 40 percent of the construction work has been completed and the country has pumped some $1 billion into it.
Bulgaria, which imports some 80 percent of its energy resources, relies on its Soviet-made nuclear plant at Kozloduy for more than 40 percent of the country's needs.
The Kozloduy plant has four old 440-megawatt reactors and two more modern 1,000-megawatt reactors. -- Liliana Semerdjieva, Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-91188
